title: Fission

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Moderator
items.clue: Slows fast neutrons in a reactor core.

items.label: Chain reaction
items.clue: Neutrons released by one event go on to cause further events.

items.label: Control rods
items.clue: Absorb neutrons; moved in or out of the core to adjust the rate.

items.label: Critical mass
items.clue: The smallest quantity of fissile material in which a self-sustaining series of fissions can occur.

questions.stem: Some very heavy nuclides, such as californium-252, can undergo spontaneous fission, whereas uranium-235 in a reactor undergoes neutron-induced fission. Which statement about spontaneous fission is correct?

options.text: Energy is released as kinetic energy of an α particle that breaks off the nucleus.
Energy is released only once the material is hot enough for its nuclei to shake apart.
No energy is released, as no neutron has been absorbed to supply the energy.
Energy is released when the nucleus splits into two fragments of comparable mass.

questions.stem: A chain reaction of uranium-235 fission in a reactor core is proceeding at a steady rate. Which condition is being met?

options.text: On average, exactly one of the neutrons from each fission causes a further fission.
Each fission releases exactly one neutron, which goes on to cause a further fission.
The fission fragments split again in turn, each one releasing further neutrons.
The moderator absorbs the surplus neutrons, leaving one per fission to continue the chain.

questions.explanation: Some neutrons escape and some are absorbed without causing fission. If on average exactly one neutron from each fission causes another fission, every generation has the same number of fissions and the rate is steady.

questions.stem: In a gas-cooled reactor, the uranium fuel rods sit in channels through a large block of graphite, which is the moderator. Carbon dioxide gas carries thermal energy from the core. What is the role of the graphite?

options.text: It slows fast neutrons by collisions, as slow neutrons are more likely to cause fission.
It absorbs surplus neutrons from the fuel, so that the rate of fission is kept under control.
It speeds up the neutrons so that they hit uranium nuclei hard enough to split them.
It moderates the temperature of the core, stopping the fuel from overheating.

questions.stem: A fission of uranium-235 produces barium-141 (¹⁴¹₅₆Ba) and krypton-92 (⁹²₃₆Kr). The heaviest stable isotopes of these elements are barium-138 (¹³⁸₅₆Ba) and krypton-86 (⁸⁶₃₆Kr). Which decay are barium-141 and krypton-92 expected to undergo?

options.text: β⁺ decay, which converts a surplus neutron into a proton
α decay, which carries the surplus neutrons away
β⁻ decay, which turns a surplus neutron into a proton
γ decay only, as nuclei formed by fission are stable

questions.explanation: Barium-141 has 85 neutrons against at most 82 in stable barium, and krypton-92 has 56 against at most 50. In β⁻ decay a neutron changes into a proton, reducing the neutron excess; both nuclides are β⁻ emitters.

questions.stem: In one neutron-induced fission of uranium-235, ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n. The atomic masses are 235.043928 u for uranium-235, 140.914403 u for barium-141 and 91.926173 u for krypton-92, and the mass of a neutron is 1.008665 u (the electron masses cancel). Take 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV c⁻², 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. How much energy is released in this fission?

In a reactor core, each fission of uranium-235 releases 2.5 neutrons on average. Of these, on average 0.7 escape from the core and 0.8 are absorbed by the control rods and other materials without causing fission. What happens to the rate of fission?

options.text: It increases: each fission releases more neutrons than the one it absorbed.
It stays constant: on average one neutron per fission causes a fission.
It decreases: control rods absorb neutrons and so shut the reaction down.
It increases: the energy released heats the fuel, so that more nuclei split.

questions.explanation: Of the 2.5 neutrons, 0.7 + 0.8 = 1.5 do not cause fission, leaving 2.5 − 1.5 = 1.0 per fission that do. Each generation has the same number of fissions, so the rate is steady.

questions.stem: Pushing the control rods further into a reactor core reduces its power output. Why?

options.text: They slow neutrons down, so the neutrons are less able to split nuclei.
They absorb thermal energy, cooling the fuel so that fewer nuclei split.
They absorb the fission fragments, which would otherwise split again.
They absorb neutrons, so fewer neutrons are left to cause fission.

questions.explanation: Control rods contain strong neutron absorbers such as boron or cadmium. Inserting them further removes more neutrons, so on average fewer than one neutron per fission causes another fission and the fission rate falls.

questions.stem: Spent fuel rods taken out of a reactor are stored for several years under a few metres of water in a pool. No chain reaction takes place in the pool, yet the pool water has to be cooled continuously. Why does the water need cooling?

options.text: The rods still hold the thermal energy they gained in the core, which leaks out only slowly.
Keeping the rods cold slows down the decay of their fission products, making them safer.
Radiation from the rods makes the water radioactive, and the water's decay heats it.
The radioactive fission products keep decaying, and their decay energy heats the rods.

questions.stem: In the fission ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁰₅₄Xe + ⁹⁴₃₈Sr + 2¹₀n, the binding energies per nucleon are 7.59 MeV for uranium-235, 8.29 MeV for xenon-140 and 8.59 MeV for strontium-94. A free neutron has no binding energy. Take 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J. How much energy is released in this fission?
questions.explanation: The energy released is the increase in total binding energy: [140(8.29) + 94(8.59)] − 235(7.59) = 1968.06 − 1783.65 = 184.41 MeV, which is 184.41 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J = 2.95 × 10⁻¹¹ J.

questions.stem: A sphere of pure uranium-235 has a mass slightly below the critical mass: a chain reaction started in it dies away. Which change, keeping the same mass of uranium-235, could allow it to sustain a chain reaction?

options.text: Place a strong neutron source beside the sphere so more fissions start
Heat the sphere strongly, so that its nuclei vibrate hard enough to split
Surround the sphere with a material that reflects escaping neutrons back into it
Cut the sphere into small pieces to expose more of its surface to neutrons

questions.explanation: Below the critical mass too many neutrons escape through the surface. A reflector returns some of them to the uranium, so more neutrons per fission go on to cause fission; enough reflection raises this to one, and the chain becomes self-sustaining.

questions.stem: In a pressurized water reactor, water pumped through the core (the primary coolant) becomes radioactive, but the water turned into steam to drive the turbine does not. What makes this possible?

options.text: The primary water mixes with cooler secondary water in the heat exchanger, which dilutes it until it is no longer radioactive.
The circuits are separate: energy is conducted through heat-exchanger tube walls to water that does not enter the core.
Boiling the water into steam in the heat exchanger destroys the radioactivity the water picked up in the core.
The tube walls absorb the radiation from the primary water, which would otherwise make the water in the secondary circuit radioactive.

questions.stem: High-level waste from a reactor contains caesium-137, a fission product with a half-life of 30 years. The waste is kept in a store for 90 years. What percentage of the initial caesium-137 activity remains at the end of this time?
questions.explanation: 90 years is 90 ÷ 30 = 3 half-lives. The activity halves three times: 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5%.
